headline: Pilbara Minerals crashes 7.4% to close at $4.52 as the ASX drops broadly, while the Iran war drags on and the RBA looks set to hike rates again before year's end.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara got hammered today, dropping 7.4% to $4.52 — its worst single-day move in the portfolio. There's no single headline to blame, but lithium prices remain under sustained pressure as global EV demand growth slows and Chinese supply floods the market. This is the continuation of a painful structural trend for the lithium sector, not a one-day blip.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two bounced 2.76% last night despite news that ex-UK Rockstar employees filed an unfair dismissal lawsuit related to GTA VI development. Markets shrugged off the legal noise — GTA VI hype remains the dominant narrative and investor sentiment stayed positive.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google edged up 0.61% last night in a generally soft market. No specific catalyst — the stock is holding up well as AI competition headlines continue to swirl, with OpenAI's GPT-6 launch this week keeping the sector in focus.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft nudged up a modest 0.16% last night. Questions are being asked about whether its strong earnings run can continue, but the market's short answer for now is yes — it remains one of the most profitable companies on the planet and AI tailwinds are real.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS eked out a small gain today, closing up 0.15% to $522.71, even as the broader ASX fell. It tracks the entire US share market and is essentially mirroring last night's US session where a few big names held up despite index weakness.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI dipped 0.37% today in a quiet session. No major AI-specific catalysts on the ASX side — the ETF is treading water after a tough run. It's still down nearly 14% from your total invested amount, reflecting how much AI stocks have pulled back from their peaks.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG slipped 0.45% today as the ASX broadly sold off, finishing down 0.89%. As a diversified multi-asset fund with heavy global equity exposure, VDHG moves with the market — today's dip reflects general risk-off sentiment around rate hike fears and Middle East tensions.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE was completely flat today at $93.02 — no movement. Emerging markets are caught between competing forces: a weaker AUD (which helps returns) and global risk-off sentiment (which hurts). Result: a quiet standoff.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — Pilbara Minerals crashes 7.4%
watch_today.detail: A brutal session for Pilbara, now sitting at $4.52 and down nearly 33% from what you paid. The long-term lithium thesis depends on EV demand recovering and Chinese oversupply easing — neither is happening quickly. That said, selling now locks in the loss at the worst possible time in the cycle. For a long-term holder, the call is to sit tight and wait for the lithium cycle to turn — but be prepared for more pain before that happens.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — AI ETF still underwater, down 14%
watch_today.detail: GXAI dipped again today and is your second-biggest loss at -$41.47. The AI sector is going through a reality-check phase after sky-high valuations in 2024-25. OpenAI's GPT-6 launch this week is a reminder the technology is still advancing fast — the long-term case for AI stocks isn't broken, just delayed. Hold and let the thesis play out.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hikes looming — watch your interest rate exposure
watch_today.detail: Multiple major banks are now tipping two more RBA rate hikes before the end of 2026, on top of three already delivered this year. This is putting pressure on the broader ASX — higher rates hurt growth stocks and consumer spending. Your VDHG and VGE holdings have some exposure here. Nothing to act on, but keep an eye on the next RBA meeting.

watch_today.title: TTWO — GTA VI legal noise, but long-term story intact
watch_today.detail: Ex-UK Rockstar employees have sued Take-Two for unfair dismissal over GTA VI development. The market ignored it (stock up 2.76% last night) and rightly so — employment disputes don't derail a $2B+ game franchise. You're still down 6.5% overall on TTWO, but GTA VI remains a potential blockbuster catalyst. Hold.

watch_today.title: MSFT — Earnings quality in focus, but holding strong
watch_today.detail: A Yahoo Finance piece this week asks whether Microsoft can keep delivering at its current profit levels. The short answer: it's well-positioned with Azure cloud and Copilot AI products, but growth expectations are sky-high. You're up 11% on your MSFT position — no reason to change anything here. Hold for the long run.

watch_today.title: Middle East conflict pushing oil and gold — watch inflation impact
watch_today.detail: Oil is sitting at US$100.75/barrel (down slightly today but still elevated) and gold has surged to US$4,389 — a safe-haven rally. The Iran-Israel conflict is showing no signs of ending, with Trump advisers now privately acknowledging it could run through to end of his term. Sustained high oil prices feed into inflation, which means rates stay higher for longer everywhere — including Australia.

world.summary: The Middle East conflict is deepening with no end in sight, Trump is escalating his battle for voter data ahead of US midterms, and oil and gold are surging on geopolitical fears.

stories.title: Trump advisers privately fear Iran war could last through end of presidential term
stories.why_it_matters: According to the Wall Street Journal, Trump's top advisers are now confronting the real possibility that the US military involvement in the Iran conflict could drag on for years — potentially through the end of his presidential term. That's a significant shift from early optimism about a quick resolution. A prolonged Middle East war keeps oil prices elevated (WTI crude is at US$100.75/barrel right now), stokes inflation globally, and keeps financial markets on edge. For everyday Australians, that means higher petrol prices and ongoing cost-of-living pressure.

stories.title: Oil, gas prices surge as Middle East conflict fears escalate
stories.why_it_matters: Energy markets are rattled by the ongoing Israel-Iran conflict, with oil and gas prices jumping sharply. Gold has also surged to US$4,389/oz — investors are piling into safe-haven assets. The BBC reports that borrowing costs are also rising in response, as markets price in prolonged instability. Higher energy costs feed directly into everything from groceries to airline tickets, making life more expensive for ordinary people.

stories.title: Iran faces strategic dilemma as war of attrition drags on
stories.why_it_matters: Middle East Eye reports that Iran is caught in a difficult strategic position — it's taking military and economic damage but can't easily back down without losing face domestically. The analysis suggests neither side has an obvious path to a clean victory, pointing to a long, grinding conflict. This matters globally because Iran is a major oil producer and any escalation risks supply disruptions that would send prices even higher.

stories.title: Trump's DOJ escalates battle with US states over voter data ahead of midterms
stories.why_it_matters: The US Department of Justice is threatening states that refuse to hand over detailed voter registration data, part of Trump's push to use a voter-screening tool that courts have blocked 23 times. The NYT reports this is raising serious alarms about federal overreach into state election administration ahead of November's midterm elections. A new PBS poll also found that few Americans trust either political campaigns or Trump himself right now — adding to political tensions heading into a crucial election cycle.

stories.title: Trump proposes $5,000 cash payments to Americans — at a cost of over $1 trillion
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration is floating a plan to send US$5,000 cheques to American households, but the NYT reports it would cost over US$1 trillion. Critics say it would explode the national debt and potentially reignite inflation just as the Federal Reserve is trying to keep it under control. If the US runs even hotter deficits, it puts upward pressure on global interest rates — which has knock-on effects for Australian borrowing costs and markets.

markets.summary: The ASX dropped 0.89% today to 8,741, dragged down by rate hike fears and global risk-off sentiment. Last night's US session was also soft — the S&P 500 fell 0.58% and the NASDAQ slid 0.65%. Oil is pulling back slightly but remains above US$100. Gold is surging as a safe haven. The Aussie dollar slipped to US71.7c.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Broad sell-off today — rate hike fears and Middle East jitters weighed on the market.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session: modest losses as the market digested elevated oil prices and geopolitical risk.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night's session: tech pulled back slightly despite individual bright spots like TTWO.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil eased slightly but remains above US$100 — Middle East conflict keeping a floor under prices.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold surging to record territory as investors seek safe havens amid geopolitical and inflation fears.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar weakened — traders see more RBA rate hikes coming but global risk-off is hurting.

politics.summary: The RBA's rate hike campaign is looking increasingly painful, with multiple big banks now tipping two more increases before 2027. Inflation isn't budging the way the RBA hoped, putting mortgage holders under even more pressure.

stories.title: RBA's three 2026 rate hikes aren't working — and more are coming
stories.why_it_matters: The Guardian reports that despite the RBA already lifting interest rates three times in 2026, inflation is stubbornly refusing to fall in line with their targets. The article suggests the central bank is running out of easy options — more hikes hurt households but not acting risks inflation becoming entrenched. Anyone with a variable-rate mortgage is bearing the brunt of this, with repayments already significantly higher than two years ago.

stories.title: Major banks tip two more rate rises before 2027
stories.why_it_matters: At least one major Australian bank is now formally forecasting two additional RBA rate hikes before the end of 2026, on top of the three already delivered. That would push the cash rate even higher and translate to hundreds more dollars per month on an average mortgage. For property investors and homeowners alike, this is the key economic story of the year — the rate pain isn't over yet.

stories.title: CommBank: Higher rates, harder choices ahead for the Australian economy
stories.why_it_matters: CommBank's own economics team published a note flagging that Australia faces difficult trade-offs: keep hiking rates to beat inflation and risk tipping the economy into a sharper slowdown, or pause and risk inflation staying sticky. They're framing this as genuinely hard for the RBA — not a clear-cut call either way. This uncertainty is one reason the ASX has been volatile, as investors try to price in an unclear rate outlook.

ai.summary: AI regulation is the big theme globally this week — Australia, the UK, the EU, and the US are all wrestling with how to govern AI, especially in healthcare. Meanwhile, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra and US agencies have accused six Chinese AI firms of stealing training data from Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Grok.

stories.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra — its most powerful model yet for workplace use
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI has officially launched GPT-6, branded as 'Astra', positioning it as a next-generation AI built specifically for work tasks. This is the successor to GPT-4 and is designed to handle complex, multi-step work tasks more reliably — think drafting legal documents, coding full applications, or running research autonomously. For anyone who uses AI tools at work, this is a meaningful upgrade. It also keeps Google (your GOOG holding) and Microsoft (MSFT, which partners with OpenAI) at the centre of the most important tech race of the decade.

stories.title: US agencies accuse six Chinese AI firms of stealing model data from Claude, GPT, Gemini and Grok
stories.why_it_matters: US government agencies have formally accused six Chinese AI companies of systematically 'siphoning' — essentially stealing — training data and outputs from Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's GPT, Google's Gemini, and Elon Musk's Grok. The accusation is that these firms fed the Western AI models' outputs back into their own training pipelines to fast-track their capabilities without doing the underlying research work. This escalates AI as a geopolitical battleground between the US and China, and could trigger new sanctions or restrictions on Chinese tech firms.

stories.title: Australia unveils AI regulation framework — what it means for businesses
stories.why_it_matters: Australia has released new AI regulation guidelines that will directly affect how companies use AI in their operations — with implications for risk management, compliance, and liability. iTWire reports that businesses will need to update their risk registers to account for AI-specific exposures, covering things like algorithmic bias, data privacy, and automated decision-making. For any Australian business using AI tools (which is increasingly all of them), this is worth understanding.

stories.title: EU grapples with AI 'extinction risk' warnings — and tries to stay calm
stories.why_it_matters: Politico reports that the European Union is quietly wrestling with how seriously to take warnings from AI researchers that advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or even existential risks. The piece describes internal EU debates about whether their AI Act — already the world's most comprehensive AI law — goes far enough. The EU is trying to balance not overreacting to speculative risks while also not being caught flat-footed if those risks prove real. It's a sign of how seriously governments are now taking AI safety as models become more powerful.

stories.title: Robots protest to demand better AI regulation — and the irony is real
stories.why_it_matters: In what might be the most surreal story of the week: robots physically protested at an AI regulation event, demanding better rules to govern AI development. The South China Morning Post reports this was a staged demonstration, but it highlights how the AI regulation debate has gone truly mainstream — even the machines are getting in on the act. It's a quirky reminder that public awareness of AI governance is now at a level that would have seemed science fiction just a few years ago.

sport.summary: NRL Finals Week 1 kicks off tonight with Rabbitohs vs Knights, and Wayne Bennett has issued a warning about Latrell Mitchell. The AFL finals are heating up with key injury and team selection news. The US Open is generating debate about late-night finishes and potential scoring system changes.

stories.title: NRL Finals Week 1 is here — Wayne Bennett warns on Latrell, Knights get boost
stories.why_it_matters: NRL Finals Week 1 gets underway tonight (Friday, 7:50pm) with Rabbitohs hosting the Knights at Allianz Stadium. Fox Sports reports that South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett has put the Knights on notice about Latrell Mitchell, while Newcastle has received a confirmed squad boost ahead of the clash. The weekend also features Warriors vs Dolphins (Saturday 4:05pm), Sharks vs Cowboys (Saturday 7:50pm), and Panthers vs Roosters (Sunday 4:05pm). Penrith's Nathan Cleary says the Panthers are 'savouring finals time' as they chase another premiership run.

stories.title: AFL finals: Geelong make official call on young gun; Lions star misses semis
stories.why_it_matters: Heading into AFL semi-finals, Fox Sports reports Geelong have made an official selection decision on a young gun (team named), while Brisbane Lions have confirmed a key player has failed to recover in time for the semis. AFL also issued a warning to clubs about trading for suspended Sydney Swans players — any club that acquires a currently-suspended player risks inheriting that suspension, which could be a costly trap in the trade period.

stories.title: Collingwood land their big forward fish; Jack Bailey turns down top-four money
stories.why_it_matters: Collingwood have officially secured a highly sought-after big forward in what The Age calls a major AFL trade coup. Meanwhile, Jack Bailey has reportedly turned down an offer that would have made him one of the top three or four paid players in the AFL — a remarkable decision that has stunned the football world. No details yet on which club Bailey rejected or where he's headed, but it's a big story heading into the trade period.

stories.title: US Open: Alcaraz knocked out in quarter-finals, late-night finishes under fire
stories.why_it_matters: Carlos Alcaraz, one of the world's top-ranked tennis players, has been knocked out of the US Open quarter-finals — a result that has commentators pointing out just how remarkable Roger Federer's multiple US Open titles really were. Separately, The Australian is reporting that matches finishing at 3:30am in New York are 'killing US tennis' — it's bad for fans, players, and broadcasters. The Australian Open has weighed in on whether it will keep five-set tennis for its 2027 tournament, with a statement expected to confirm its format.
